summary: Specifies IPv4 compatibility mechanisms for IPv6 hosts and routers: dual stack and configured tunneling. Dual stack means implementing both IP versions, and configured tunneling carries IPv6 packets across IPv4 networks. It is a standards-track document.

eli5.summary: Some computers can speak both old and new internet languages, which is dual stack. Others hide new-language letters inside old-language envelopes to cross old roads.

questions: how does ipv6 over ipv4 tunneling work
what is the ipv6 tunnel mtu
subtitle: Dual stack and configured tunnels: the two basic ways IPv6 hosts and routers stay compatible with IPv4.

tldr.problem: IPv6 had to be deployed alongside a large installed base of IPv4 hosts and routers, so IPv6 nodes needed ways to keep working with IPv4.
tldr.mechanism: Dual stack gives a node complete IPv4 and IPv6 implementations. Configured tunneling wraps IPv6 packets in IPv4 headers (protocol 41) between manually configured endpoints so they can cross IPv4 routing infrastructure.
tldr.outcome: The RFC makes these two mechanisms the core of a transition toolbox and specifies MTU, fragmentation, error handling and source-address checks so tunnels interoperate and are not an easy way around ingress filtering.

today: RFC 4213 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2005. It obsoletes RFC 2893, and the metadata lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: A Transition Toolbox
sections.content:
The RFC starts from the idea that a successful IPv6 transition depends on compatibility with the large installed base of IPv4 hosts and routers. It expects most nodes to need that compatibility for a long time, and perhaps indefinitely.

It defines two mechanisms: dual IP layer (dual stack) and configured tunneling of IPv6 over IPv4. They are meant as the core of a growing transition toolbox that sites use as needed. Other transition mechanisms, including other tunneling schemes, are outside its scope.

The vocabulary: an IPv4-only node implements only IPv4, an IPv6/IPv4 node implements both, and an IPv6-only node implements only IPv6 (its operation is not covered here).
sections.eli5: Moving to a new language takes a long time, so there is a toolbox of tricks to help old and new speakers understand each other. This memo describes the first two tools.

sections.title: Dual Stack Nodes
sections.content:
The most straightforward way to stay compatible with IPv4-only nodes is to provide a complete IPv4 implementation too. An IPv6/IPv4 node can send and receive both kinds of packets, so it talks to IPv4 nodes with IPv4 and to IPv6 nodes with IPv6. A node may run with only IPv4 enabled, only IPv6 enabled, or both, and MAY offer a switch to disable either.

Addresses come from each family's own mechanisms: IPv4 addresses from, for example, DHCP, and IPv6 addresses from, for example, stateless autoconfiguration or DHCPv6.

For names, resolver libraries on such nodes MUST handle both AAAA (IPv6) and A (IPv4) records. The resolver MAY order results to favor IPv6 or IPv4. Applications SHOULD be able to say which family they want, and when they have no preference or ask for both, the resolver MUST NOT filter out any records. The ordering rules themselves are out of scope; see RFC 3484.
sections.eli5: A dual stack computer is like a person who speaks both languages. It uses whichever one the other side understands.

sections.title: Encapsulation and the IPv4 Header
sections.content:
In configured tunneling, the tunnel entry node (the encapsulator) puts an IPv4 header in front of the IPv6 packet. The exit node (the decapsulator) reassembles it if needed, strips the IPv4 header and processes the IPv6 packet. Tunnel endpoint addresses come from configuration stored for each tunnel, and all tunnels are assumed to be bidirectional. Tunnels can be router-to-router, host-to-router, host-to-host or router-to-host, but configured tunneling is most likely router-to-router because endpoints must be set up explicitly.

The outer IPv4 header is built with Version 4, header length 5 (no options), Type of Service 0 unless otherwise specified, and protocol 41. The source is an address of the encapsulator, and it SHOULD be possible to configure it administratively. The destination is the tunnel endpoint's IPv4 address. Total length is the IPv6 payload length plus a constant 60 bytes.
sections.eli5: Put the new-language letter inside an old-language envelope, address the envelope to the other end of the tunnel, and the old roads will carry it. At the far end, someone opens the envelope.

sections.title: Tunnel MTU and Fragmentation
sections.content:
An encapsulator MUST NOT treat the tunnel as a link with an MTU of about 64 kilobytes. That would cause more fragmentation than needed, force the decapsulator to reassemble IPv4 fragments, and assume a decapsulator able to defragment and receive such large IPv6 packets. Instead it uses one of two approaches, selectable per tunnel endpoint if both are implemented.

Static MTU: the tunnel is a link with a fixed MTU. The default MUST be between 1280 and 1480 bytes inclusive, and SHOULD be 1280. The Don't Fragment bit MUST NOT be set in the outer header. A larger fixed MTU must not be configured unless the decapsulator is known to cope.

Dynamic MTU is OPTIONAL. The encapsulator tracks the IPv4 path MTU with Path MTU Discovery (RFC 1191) and uses that value minus the 20-byte IPv4 header as the tunnel MTU. Because every IPv6 link needs an MTU of at least 1280 bytes, a small path MTU is handled by the algorithm in the code box. The RFC warns that dynamic MTU is subject to path MTU black holes if ICMPv4 messages are dropped by firewalls or never generated.
sections.eli5: The envelope must fit through every doorway on the road. You either always use a small safe size, or you measure the narrowest doorway first.

sections.title: Hop Limit and ICMP Errors
sections.content:
Tunnels are modeled as a single hop from the IPv6 point of view, so traceroute-style tools do not see them. The encapsulator and decapsulator decrement the IPv6 hop limit by 1 when forwarding, as for any other link. The IPv4 TTL of the outer header is chosen in an implementation-dependent way.

Routers inside the tunnel may send ICMPv4 errors back to the encapsulator. These matter only for dynamic MTU. A 'packet too big' message updates the recorded path MTU. For other errors, older IPv4 routers return only 8 bytes beyond the IPv4 header, too little to include the IPv6 addresses. When enough of the original packet is returned, the encapsulator MAY turn the error into an ICMPv6 message to the source, such as 'unreachable' with code 'address unreachable'. It is also useful to log the error as tunnel-related.

When the path MTU is exceeded and not enough bytes come back, there will be at least two packet drops instead of one, since both the router and the host must learn the MTU.
sections.eli5: To the people sending letters, the tunnel looks like one short step. If the envelope bounces back, the tunnel entrance tries to tell the sender what went wrong.

sections.title: Decapsulation and Link-Local Rules
sections.content:
A node that gets an IPv4 datagram addressed to itself with protocol field 41 treats it as a potential tunnel packet. It checks it against its configured tunnels, reassembles it if fragmented, removes the IPv4 header and hands the IPv6 packet to the IPv6 layer. The IPv6 length must come from the IPv6 payload length, since the IPv4 packet may be padded.

The decapsulator MUST verify that the IPv4 source address is the configured address of the tunnel's other end. Non-matching packets MUST be discarded, and an ICMP message SHOULD NOT be generated. It MUST be capable of an IPv6 MRU of at least the larger of 1500 bytes and its largest IPv6 interface MTU, and of reassembling IPv4 packets up to the larger of 1500 bytes and its largest IPv4 interface MTU. After decapsulation it MUST silently discard packets with invalid IPv6 source addresses, at least multicast (FF00::/8), loopback (::1), IPv4-compatible (::/96, excluding the unspecified address) and IPv4-mapped (::ffff:0:0/96) addresses.

Configured tunnels are IPv6 interfaces, so they MUST have link-local addresses. One option is the prefix FE80::/64 followed by an interface identifier of zeros and the 32-bit IPv4 address. For Neighbor Discovery, tunnels have no link-layer address: senders SHOULD NOT include link-layer address options and receivers MUST ignore them. Implementations MUST answer Neighbor Unreachability Detection probes and SHOULD send them.
sections.eli5: At the far end, the mail clerk first checks that the envelope came from the expected sender. If not, it is thrown away quietly without telling the sender that the clerk exists.

sections.title: Spoofing and Tunnel Security
sections.content:
A tunnel is a link, but its threat model differs because it potentially includes the whole Internet. Without checks, an attacker could send a packet with its own real outer IPv4 source, the decapsulator as outer destination, and a forged inner IPv6 source such as a node close to the decapsulator. IPv4 and IPv6 ingress filtering alone would not catch it, so the tunnel could bypass filtering.

The mitigations are the decapsulator rules: the IPv4 source MUST match the configured tunnel endpoint, obviously invalid IPv6 sources MUST be discarded, IPv4 ingress filtering (strict RPF-like) MAY be done but is RECOMMENDED to be off by default, and IPv6 ingress filtering should be performed. The RFC calls the first check vital, since to avoid it an attacker must know and spoof the tunnel source.

This leaves some risk. If it matters, use a tunnel with authentication, such as IPsec (preferable) or GRE with a pre-configured key. Shorter tunnels are preferable to ones spanning the Internet. Dropped packets should not reveal the tunnel's existence, so ICMP errors should follow how the node treats unknown protocols.
sections.eli5: A tunnel is a secret door, so the guard at the end checks every visitor's name against a list. Better still is to also check their signature.

sections.title: Changes From RFC 2893
sections.content:
The changes aim to simplify the document to mechanisms in wide-spread use. The biggest removals are automatic tunneling and IPv4-compatible addresses, because RFC 3056 gives each node with a global IPv4 address a /48 IPv6 prefix. The default configured tunnel using an IPv4 anycast address, the mention of 6over4, source address selection (now covered by RFC 3484), unidirectional tunnels and A6 references were also removed.

Additions include separate treatment of static and dynamic MTU, minimal IPv4 reassembly and IPv6 MRU rules, stronger source address checks (both IPv4 and IPv6 MUST be checked), a SHOULD for a configurable tunnel source address, and a rewritten security section.
sections.eli5: The old rulebook had extra tricks that most people did not use. This version trims it down and adds clearer safety rules.

cells: Set unless the path MTU would give less than 1280

data.title: Forwarding an IPv6 packet into the tunnel
data.code:
if (IPv4 path MTU - 20) is less than 1280
        if packet is larger than 1280 bytes
                Send ICMPv6 "packet too big" with MTU = 1280.
                Drop packet.
        else
                Encapsulate but do not set the Don't Fragment
                flag in the IPv4 header.
else
        if packet is larger than (IPv4 path MTU - 20)
                Send ICMPv6 "packet too big" with
                MTU = (IPv4 path MTU - 20).
                Drop packet.
        else
                Encapsulate and set the Don't Fragment flag
                in the IPv4 header.
endif
